title: Shimano Sells Not One Bike. So How Does It Make ¥466.2 Billion a Year?
description:
In February 1921, in Sakai, Osaka Prefecture, a young man opened an ironworks, and the next year it began making freewheels for bicycle rear wheels. More than a hundred years later, Nikkei estimates that about 85 percent of the world's sports bike components come from this company, yet it does not sell a single complete bicycle. In 2025 its revenue was 466.2 billion yen: about three quarters from bicycle components and nearly a quarter from fishing tackle.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. The people in them are unidentified ordinary figures; the founder, members of the Shimano family and any logos are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-31

chapters.open-you: February 1921: an ironworks opens in Sakai
chapters.rule-unknown: One line: never compete with your customers
chapters.abroad-ny: 1965: the company goes to New York
chapters.boom-surge: At 100 years old, revenue up 44 percent
chapters.bust-freeze: 2023: a new plant opens, but bikes won't sell
chapters.lange-reveal: The biggest customer is in Stuttgart

t001.text: Your road bike's derailleur very likely comes from one Japanese company.

t002.text: Nikkei estimates it makes about 85 percent of sports bike parts worldwide.

t003.text: Yet it doesn't sell a single complete bike.

t004.text: In February 1921, a young man in the city of Sakai opened an ironworks.

t005.text: Its smiths were fixing imported bikes back in the Meiji era.

t006.text: Next year, it began making small bike gears.

t007.text: Thirty years on, it absorbed Shimano Bicycle.

t008.text: The name says bicycle. So why doesn't it sell bikes now?

t009.text: Later, some bike makers said parts took 400 days to arrive.

t010.text: Later, an American commission came looking for it.

t011.text: This file goes through its 105 years of books.

t012.text: Shimano sells no bikes. How do others' bikes earn it money?

t013.text: No record says what that firm did.

t014.text: What I could find: The Straits Times quoting a Shimano family member:

t015.text: The founder said: never, ever compete with your customers.

t016.text: I can't find when he said it;

t017.text: the founder died in 1958, but the saying stayed.

t018.text: If you made bikes, would you buy parts from a rival bike seller?

t019.text: I'd guess not. That's my own inference; that one line is all I can find.

t020.text: One company history says all six presidents to date have been from the Shimano family.

t021.text: That first small gear is a freewheel.

t022.text: It's why your wheels keep turning when you stop pedaling mid-ride.

t023.text: But if it won't compete, where are the customers?

t024.text: Overseas. In March 1965, it opened a company in New York.

t025.text: In 1967, a German firm became its main German distributor.

t027.text: In 1970, it also began making fishing reels, a side business that's still going today.

t029.text: In 1972, Americans bought more bicycles than cars.

t030.text: A Europe arm in West Germany, too;

t031.text: an American company directory says it started with two employees.

t032.text: Two people. Probably taking turns on the phone.

t033.text: In 1973, it opened its first assembly plant outside Japan, in Singapore;

t035.text: In 1974, it opened a sales office in California.

t036.text: That directory's verdict: it caught the American boom just right.

t037.text: A veteran U.S. mechanic wrote: its top group,

t039.text: but only truly took off in 1984. What happened that year?

t040.text: On that top group, it added something new: indexed shifting.

t041.text: Shifting used to be by feel; indexed means one click, one gear.

t042.text: Today, when one click puts you in gear, you're using that idea.

t043.text: But others made good parts too. So what extra did it have?

t045.text: That directory says it sold shifters and derailleurs as one matched set

t047.text: In my view, that move beat any single new part.

t048.text: Sold as a set, how could rivals get in?

t049.text: In 1987, a new Chicago company appeared, making twist-grip shifters.

t050.text: The small firm sued Shimano in California over antitrust.

t051.text: In 1991, the two settled out of court, on undisclosed terms.

t052.text: After that, makers could mix in others' parts.

t053.text: In the early 1990s, it also put shifting and braking in one lever.

t054.text: In 1997, America's product safety commission issued a notice,

t055.text: and the star of it: a crank.

t056.text: A crank is the metal arm that turns as you pedal.

t057.text: It said over a million were in North America,

t058.text: with over 630 reports of them breaking, and 22 people hurt.

t059.text: Whose bikes were these cranks on?

t060.text: Over 200 bike models, under at least 49 brands.

t061.text: Reports then said 2.5 million mountain bikes would be recalled in North America and Europe.

t062.text: On the list was a name you surely know: Giant.

t063.text: To me, this is the flip side of everyone using it: one crank fails, all brands fail.

t064.text: Surprisingly, it wasn't over. In 1999, the commission announced

t065.text: Shimano's U.S. arm agreed to a civil penalty of 150,000 dollars.

t066.text: The charge wasn't breaking cranks. It was reporting late:

t067.text: it knew people had been hurt, but didn't report in time.

t068.text: Shimano denied any crank defect and any reporting violation.

t070.text: hold that figure for another fine.

t071.text: So what's its role in Taiwan?

t072.text: In 2002, it set up Shimano Taiwan in Taichung; the arm you meet in Taiwan is the one selling parts.

t073.text: What really put it on a roller coaster was 2020.

t074.text: When the pandemic hit, bike demand shot up.

t075.text: That August, a Nikkei commentary was headlined:

t076.text: This bike parts maker's market value overtook Nissan Motor.

t077.text: A gear maker worth more than a carmaker? I read that headline twice.

t079.text: Here come the 400 days: the Financial Times quoted Western bike makers:

t080.text: high-end parts took that long from order to delivery.

t081.text: It also said Taiwan's Giant and Merida were both hit;

t082.text: the same report said a small U.S. maker's first-half deliveries fell 80 percent.

t083.text: If you queued for a new bike those two years,

t084.text: this is part of the reason.

t086.text: Its PR said capacity had been greatly expanded,

t087.text: fourth-quarter 2020 output was the highest in its history,

t088.text: and urged customers to order early.

t089.text: It turned 100 in 2021; revenue rose 44 percent,

t091.text: Its new president told Nikkei of investing about 20 billion yen in a new Singapore plant.

t092.text: How high did the boom go?

t094.text: in pre-pandemic 2019, it was just 363.2 billion.

t095.text: Of every 100 yen in revenue, nearly 27 was operating profit.

t096.text: Doing that well, wouldn't you expect the good times to last?

t097.text: That October's report added one line:

t098.text: demand is steady, but showing signs of cooling.

t099.text: The cooling soon turned into a deep freeze.

t100.text: In 2023, revenue fell nearly a quarter, and operating profit was cut in half;

t101.text: bike parts alone dropped nearly 30 percent.

t102.text: The report said: the boom cooled, market stock stayed too high;

t103.text: North American bike retail stayed weak too.

t104.text: Picture it: parts rush-ordered in the pandemic became bikes,

t105.text: sitting in warehouses and shops with no buyers.

t106.text: Remember that new Singapore plant? It started running that very year.

t107.text: A decision made in the boom arrived just as things froze.

t108.text: That September, an old problem came back.

t109.text: On September 21, the commission issued another recall.

t110.text: Cranks again. This time, 11-speed bonded hollow cranks.

t112.text: 680,000 sets in the U.S., plus 80,000 in Canada.

t113.text: The notice cited 4,519 reports of cranks coming apart.

t114.text: Bike media said worldwide, it came to 2.8 million sets.

t115.text: They'd been sold for over 11 years, at 270 to 1,500 dollars a set.

t116.text: If you got its pricier cranks then,

t117.text: this notice is worth looking up.

t118.text: What did it cost it this time?

t119.text: Free inspections alone cost it a 17.6 billion yen loss that year.

t120.text: Here's the question: didn't it see the crash coming?

t121.text: It did. In 2024, chairman Yozo Shimano told Nikkei:

t122.text: We knew all along it would crash someday.

t124.text: He said at the peak, output came first, other plans waited.

t125.text: That year, revenue fell a bit more.

t127.text: This February, a U.S. court approved the crank class-action deal,

t128.text: two big bike makers were sued alongside it.

t129.text: Remember that line about ordering early?

t130.text: On March 1, Nikkei put it bluntly:

t131.text: Shimano couldn't dissuade makers from boom overproduction.

t132.text: To me, this is a parts maker's hardest problem:

t133.text: customers build the bikes, and how many isn't your call.

t134.text: Then came that commission from the start: on March 16, it showed up.

t135.text: Shimano agreed to pay an 11.5 million dollar civil penalty.

t137.text: The same as 1999: not reporting right away.

t138.text: Twenty-seven years apart; that's what bothers me most in this whole file.

t140.text: The settlement states it doesn't admit the charges;

t141.text: it adds that no injuries were reported after checks and swaps began.

t142.text: That 150,000 dollars became over 70 times as much this time.

t143.text: The day after, it filed its annual report.

t144.text: Under biggest customer, it listed a German name.

t146.text: It's Paul Lange, in Stuttgart, founded in 1949.

t147.text: Last year, it alone bought nearly 54 billion yen's worth.

t148.text: At 11.6 percent, it's Shimano's single biggest customer.

t149.text: I didn't see that answer coming.

t150.text: The prior year: under 10 percent, not even named.

t151.text: So how much did Germany grow in one year?

t152.text: Revenue in Germany rose nearly 40 percent; that same year, China fell by a third.

t153.text: Back to the opening question: it sells no bikes, so how?

t154.text: My answer: remember the founder's words?

t155.text: It doesn't compete, so makers trust its parts on their bikes;

t156.text: and agents sell them into markets like Germany.

t157.text: Fishing gear included, its 2025 revenue was 466.2 billion yen.

t158.text: Who made your bike's derailleur? Tell me in the comments.

t159.text: Every file comes with sources. To keep digging with me, subscribe.
